title: Flyweight Pattern
oneLiner: Shares the common, unchanging parts of many similar objects so a huge population of them fits comfortably in memory.

hero.name: Featherweight
hero.catchphrase: Why have a million copies when one shared core will do?
hero.power: Splits an object's data into shared (intrinsic) and unique (extrinsic) parts, so millions of instances can reuse one shared core.
hero.weakness: Splitting shared from unique state is real design work — and if that shared state is ever accidentally mutated, every 'independent' object using it corrupts at once.
hero.origin: Featherweight arrived after a text editor stored a full font, size, and color object for every single character on the page — a million-character document meant a million duplicate font objects.

story.problem: A text editor stores `{ char, font, size, color }` for every character. A million-character document allocates a million nearly-identical font/size/color objects, eating gigabytes for data that's 99% duplicated.
story.solution: Featherweight splits each character into a shared `CharacterStyle` (font, size, color — intrinsic, reused across thousands of characters) and unique per-character position (extrinsic, stored separately, cheap).
story.result: A million characters that share the same 20 styles now allocate 20 style objects total, not a million. Memory drops by orders of magnitude.

before: Each character allocates its own font/size/color object
A million characters means a million near-duplicate objects
Memory usage scales linearly with character count
after: Identical styles are shared across every character that uses them
A million characters share a small pool of style objects
Memory usage scales with unique styles, not character count

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A memory profiler shows a document consuming 2GB — almost entirely duplicate font/size/color objects.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: This document has maybe 20 distinct styles in it, but we've allocated a million style objects, one per character!

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: Featherweight appears holding one lightweight style object, gesturing at a thousand characters that all reference it.
panels.speaker: Featherweight
panels.dialogue: Stop copying the style for every character. Share ONE style object across every character that looks the same.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: A StyleFactory hands out the same CharacterStyle instance whenever the same font/size/color combo is requested.
panels.speaker: Featherweight
panels.dialogue: The style is intrinsic — shared and immutable. Only the character's position is extrinsic — unique, and cheap to store separately.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The memory profiler now shows 20 style objects total, shared across a million characters.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: 2GB dropped to under 40MB. Same document, same styles — just shared instead of duplicated.

useWhen: You need a huge number of similar objects, and memory usage is a real, measured problem.
Most of each object's state is shared and immutable (intrinsic), with only a small part being unique (extrinsic).
The shared state can be safely made immutable — no object using it should ever mutate it directly.
avoidWhen: The object count is small enough that memory isn't actually a concern — Flyweight adds complexity for no measured payoff.
Most of the object's state is genuinely unique per instance, leaving little to actually share.
The 'shared' state needs to be mutable per-instance — that breaks the sharing guarantee and causes silent bugs.
commonMistakes: Applying Flyweight before confirming memory is actually a bottleneck — this pattern trades simplicity for memory savings, so measure first.
Accidentally mutating shared (intrinsic) state, corrupting every object that references it.
Forgetting to separate extrinsic state cleanly, ending up with a factory that isn't really sharing much after all.
Using a naive equality check in the factory's cache key, causing near-duplicate keys to create redundant flyweights anyway.
explanation.realWorldExample: Text editors sharing glyph/font objects across characters, game engines sharing mesh/texture data across thousands of identical trees or bullets, and string interning in many languages (identical string literals sharing one memory location) are all Flyweight.

conversation.speaker: Featherweight
conversation.message: Caching avoids recomputation. I go further — I make MANY objects literally share the same underlying instance for their common data, splitting shared from unique state on purpose.

conversation.speaker: Featherweight
conversation.message: If that shared state is ever mutated — even once — every object referencing it changes too, silently. Intrinsic state has to stay immutable, or I turn into a very confusing bug.

codeBattle.scenario: Your forest-rendering game engine needs to draw 500,000 trees. Each tree shares the same mesh and texture but has a unique position and slight rotation, and memory is already tight.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: Featherweight shares the identical mesh/texture (intrinsic) across all 500,000 trees, storing only position/rotation (extrinsic) per tree — cutting memory dramatically.

quiz.question: What is 'intrinsic state' in the Flyweight pattern?
options: The shared, typically immutable data that many objects have in common and can reuse from one instance
The unique, per-object data that must be stored separately for each instance
A random value generated at object creation
State that only exists during a database transaction
quiz.answer: The shared, typically immutable data that many objects have in common and can reuse from one instance
quiz.explanation: Intrinsic state is exactly what gets factored out and shared across many flyweight instances.

quiz.question: What is 'extrinsic state', and where does it live?
options: The unique, per-object data (like position) that's kept separate from the shared flyweight and supplied by the caller
It's stored inside the shared flyweight object alongside intrinsic state
It doesn't exist in the Flyweight pattern
It's always stored in a database
quiz.answer: The unique, per-object data (like position) that's kept separate from the shared flyweight and supplied by the caller
quiz.explanation: Keeping extrinsic state out of the shared object is exactly what makes the sharing safe.

quiz.question: What's the biggest risk when implementing Flyweight?
options: Accidentally mutating the shared intrinsic state, which corrupts every object referencing it
Using too much memory compared to not sharing at all
Breaking type safety in a way TypeScript can't catch at compile time
quiz.answer: Accidentally mutating the shared intrinsic state, which corrupts every object referencing it
quiz.explanation: Because many objects reference the same shared instance, any mutation to it silently affects everything sharing it.

quiz.question: When should you avoid Flyweight?
options: When the number of objects is small enough that memory usage isn't actually a measured problem
When you have hundreds of thousands of similar objects
When most of the object's state can be shared safely
When memory is a confirmed bottleneck
quiz.answer: When the number of objects is small enough that memory usage isn't actually a measured problem
quiz.explanation: Flyweight adds real design complexity that should only be paid for when memory savings are actually needed.
